Lena said it plainly, the way she might have ordered a meal: she wanted Wes Tarrow dead. She sat across from Aaron in the kitchen of the house that had once belonged to her and Doug and their two girls, and she said it without crying. Aaron listened to the heart in his chest, Doug's heart, and he bought a gun.

Before any of that, Wes Tarrow had been a different man, or tried to be. He came out of prison born again, held down a job at a warehouse, coached boys' baseball on weekends. His wife Nita watched him pray and watched him clench his jaw and she dreaded both equally.

Lena Ward had been a different woman too. A recovered addict with years clean, she lived with Doug in a quiet suburb where their two young daughters grew sunburned in the yard and the kitchen smelled like toast and soap.

All of that was before Aaron Vale was told his heart would kill him within weeks. The cardiologist showed him scans the way a mechanic shows you a cracked engine block. No repair. A donor or a funeral.

After the funeral—after everything—Lena went back to cocaine. She began with a single line at a friend's house, and within days she was methodically dismantling herself, as though sobriety had been a structure she'd built around the grief and now she wanted it gone.

The crossing had a sign and a painted line. Wes's pickup hit Doug and both girls and kept going. He drove two miles, turned back, and then fled again. He could not explain the sequence to himself afterward, only that something in him had split open and each direction was wrong.

At the hospital, a doctor took Lena into a room with bad lighting and told her that her husband and both children were dead. She nodded. She asked for her purse.

Wes walked into a police station on a Tuesday morning and confessed. They sent him back to prison. Nita did not visit.

Doug's heart was transplanted into Aaron Vale, who woke in a hospital bed feeling the strangest thing—life, pushing through him, insistent, almost rude. He hadn't felt alive in months. He pressed his palm to his sternum and felt it drumming, someone else's rhythm, someone else's insistence on continuing.

He could not stop thinking about it. The heart was not his. He hired a private investigator and asked only one question: who was the donor? The investigator found the widow's name and address in three days.

Released early for reasons the system never made clear, Wes walked out on Nita and on his faith. He left his Bible on the kitchen table and took work at a motel far from home, changing sheets, fixing toilets, saying almost nothing to anyone.

Aaron followed Lena. He watched her buy groceries, watched her sit in her parked car for long stretches doing nothing. He engineered a meeting at a swimming pool—her daughters would have loved a pool, he didn't know that yet—by pretending to be a fellow member of the community recreation center. They spoke. They spoke again. They began an affair that neither of them could locate on any map of reason.

He left Della. His estranged wife had been pressing him for months to agree to be inseminated with his frozen sperm before he died, and he told her no. He told her he did not want the child she was trying to conceive. She closed the door on him and that was the end of that marriage.

Aaron tracked Wes to the motel. He raised the gun in the parking lot but could not go through with it. He fired once, wounding Wes in the shoulder, and told him to run.

Then Aaron went back to Lena and told her the truth—that he was carrying her husband's heart. She stared at him and threw him out. He sat on her porch for an hour. She opened the door and took him back.

Wes followed them to their motel. He found Aaron in the parking lot and asked him to finish the job. Aaron turned the gun on himself instead.

Lena and Wes got the dying Aaron to a hospital. The transplanted heart failed in the emergency room, Doug's heart finally giving out as though it recognized the absurdity of its journey. Wes went home to Nita. Lena, pregnant, went home alone.

The coffee was bad and the eggs were worse, but Caleb and Jody had eaten worse in their time, which was saying something given how little time they'd had. They'd been talking about robbery in the abstract, the way other people talked about weather or sports, and then Jody looked around the diner with its plate glass windows and its single cashier and said, "We're already here." Caleb felt the idea settle into him like a stone dropping into still water. They pulled their guns and stood up.

Across the city, in a different life entirely, Rollo and Marcus drove with the windows down, arguing about Thailand. "They'll kill you for a bag of powder over there," Marcus said. "Execution. Bullet in the head." Rollo shrugged. "What do they call a Quarter Pounder?" "They don't call it a Quarter Pounder." "What do they call it?" "I don't know. Something with metric." They parked and walked to the flat, stood in the corridor, and Marcus said, "A foot massage. That's what he got killed over." Rollo leaned against the wall. "It's more than a foot massage." "It's rubbing feet, Rollo." "It's intimacy. A man's woman giving another man that kind of attention—it's a violation." Marcus shook his head, recited a passage from Ezekiel, and they kicked in the door. Tobin was sitting on the couch. He didn't have time to look surprised. They took the briefcase from the table and left him slumped.

They delivered it to Otis at his bar, where the old man sat counting bills across a table from Denny, a boxer well past his prime. Otis slid the money forward. "Fifth round. You go down." Denny nodded, took the cash, and left without looking at either hitman.

Rollo went home, bought heroin from Kip, cooked it, and shot up before changing his shirt. He picked up Nadia—Otis's wife—in a borrowed car and took her to a themed diner where they ordered milkshakes and entered the dance contest. They won. She was luminous and he was flying. They went back to his place. She found the bag of heroin on the nightstand and snorted a heavy line. She dropped. Rollo screamed, drove her to Kip's living room, and they plunged a needle of adrenaline straight into her heart. She sat up gasping, eyes wide as a newborn animal.

Years earlier, a prisoner of war had come home and found a boy waiting on a porch. The man pressed a gold watch into the boy's hands. "Your father wanted you to have this," he said. "He kept it hidden the whole time. Never let them take it."

Denny won the fight. He didn't go down in the fifth. He knocked his opponent cold in the first and walked out through the service exit into a taxi. In a motel room with Marielle, he patted his pockets and felt the absence. "The watch," he said. "You left it at the flat." She stared at him. He went back. Rollo was in the kitchen. Denny saw the submachine gun on the counter, grabbed it, and fired. Rollo fell.

In the street, Denny's car met Otis's. Metal folded around them. They were dragged into the basement of a pawnshop. Denny broke his bindings, took a sword from the shop wall, and came back downstairs. Otis looked at him. "We're square," Otis said. "You leave town." Denny collected Marielle and rode out on a motorcycle.

Back in the flat, before any of that, a fourth man had been hiding in the bathroom. He came out firing a revolver. Every shot missed. Marcus called it divine intervention. In the car afterward, Rollo's gun went off. Del's head became a painting on the rear window. Marcus drove to Warren's house. A fixer directed the cleanup and handed them fresh clothes.

At the diner, Caleb and Jody held everyone at gunpoint. Marcus talked them down, handed over his wallet, kept the briefcase, and let them walk out the door.

Over eggs and burnt toast at the diner, the crew argued about what the pop song on the radio was really about. Cal said it was about a girl. Mr. Ash said it was about a gun. Mr. Birch said it was about a car, which made no sense to anyone. The waitress came by with a coffeepot and Mr. Cedar waved her off without looking up. The argument shifted to whether she deserved a tip. Cal said she'd poured three refills. Mr. Elm said pouring coffee wasn't a skill. He said it carefully, like a man who'd rehearsed being careless.

Mr. Ash drove with one hand on the wheel and the other pressing a wadded jacket against Mr. Elm's belly. Elm was screaming, a wet and animal sound that filled the car and leaked out the cracked window into traffic. Ash kept telling him he was not going to die. He said it like a prayer, like a man who needed the words more than the wounded man did. The diamonds were gone. The job had lasted sixty seconds before it fell apart, and now Elm was leaking onto the upholstery and Ash was driving too fast toward the warehouse and promising things he couldn't deliver.

They reached the warehouse first. Mr. Birch arrived minutes later, wild-eyed, and said what they were all thinking: the job had been a setup. There was an informer inside the crew. He wouldn't say who. He took the diamonds and hid them outside the building, in a drainpipe behind the dumpsters, and came back in wiping his hands on his trousers.

That morning, before the diner, Bram had handed out the aliases. He liked trees. He said it made the crew sound like a grove, like something natural. Mr. Elm, Mr. Ash, Mr. Cedar, Mr. Birch. When Birch got his name he objected. He said birch was a weak wood, a pale wood, and he wanted something with weight. Bram told him birch was flexible and that flexibility was survival. Nobody argued with Bram twice.

Mr. Cedar strolled into the warehouse like he was late for brunch. He popped the boot of his car and pulled out a patrolman, bound at the wrists and ankles, and dragged him inside. The officer's name was Doyle. He was young and his eyes were wide and wet and he kept saying please in a voice that barely carried.

Ren Vasco walked out of prison on a Tuesday morning carrying a cardboard box with his belongings. He reported to Bram and Cal that afternoon. They owed him. Seven years he'd kept his mouth shut, and they'd promised the debt would be honored. Bram gave him a drink and a chair and said he was family now. Cal said nothing. Cal never said much to men who'd done time for his father.

Left alone with the bound officer, Mr. Cedar turned the radio on. An oldie came through the speaker, something with horns and a woman's voice. Cedar danced. He moved his hips and snapped his fingers and smiled at Doyle like they were on a date. Then he cut off the officer's ear with a folding knife and doused him in petrol from a jerrican in the corner. Doyle screamed through his gag. Cedar hummed along with the radio.

From the floor, bleeding, Mr. Elm raised his gun and shot Mr. Cedar dead. The shot echoed. Elm looked at Doyle and told him he was a cop. He said the police were outside. He said they were waiting for Bram.

Weeks earlier, in a safe house kitchen, Danny Roarke had rehearsed a story about a drug bust in a public toilet. His handler Pruitt sat across the table and made him tell it again and again until the pauses fell in the right places, until the details had the texture of memory. Pruitt said a cover story wasn't something you remembered, it was something you forgot was fake.

Danny performed the anecdote for Bram, for Cal, and for Mr. Ash. Bram laughed at the right moment. Cal watched his eyes. Ash nodded. They took him onto the crew as Mr. Elm.

The robbery collapsed within a minute. Mr. Ash shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Mr. Elm beside him. Fleeing on foot, Elm hijacked a car and was shot in the stomach by the terrified driver. He shot the driver dead.

Cal returned to the warehouse and listened to Elm's account of what Cedar had done. Cal looked at the body. He looked at Doyle. Then he shot Doyle dead himself.

Bram arrived last. He walked in and named Mr. Elm as the informer. Mr. Ash refused to believe it. He turned his gun on Bram. The standoff was brief and loud. Bram, Cal, and Ash all went down. Only Ash and Elm still breathed.

Elm confessed that he was a police officer. Ash looked at him with something worse than anger. He shot Elm in the chest as the police stormed the warehouse, and Ash was cut down in the doorway, still pulling the trigger.

The snow globe slipped from Emmett Rusk's fingers as the last breath left him. It struck the marble floor of Silvermount and cracked, a slow spill of water and white glitter spreading across the cold stone. The word he whispered — *Bluebell* — hung in the empty hall, unanswered by the mirrors that lined the walls in endless reflection.

Within days, the newsreel obituaries were spooling across theater screens. They showed Emmett in his prime: shaking hands, breaking ground, standing before the Clarion building with his name on the masthead. They traced his fortune, his marriage, his campaign for governor, his defeat. They closed on his face, older and grim, and offered no explanation for his final word.

The Clarion sent a reporter named Nash to find out what it meant. His first lead was Nora — Emmett's second wife — and he tracked her to a seaside nightclub where she sat drinking gin in a back booth. When he asked about Bluebell, she laughed without pleasure and told him to go to hell. Her eyes were glassy and her hands shook, and Nash understood that whatever the word meant to her, she would not be the one to say it.

So he went backward, into the paper trail of Emmett's life, and the story opened under him like a mine shaft.

In a mining boarding house out west, Emmett's mother had signed her son over to the banker Barrow. A lodger had defaulted and left behind a mine deed that made the Rusk family suddenly, astonishingly rich. Barrow was to manage the boy and the fortune, to carry him east and raise him as a gentleman. But the boy had other ideas. He drove his sled straight into Barrow's stomach, and they took him east anyway, howling.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett seized control of the fortune and told Barrow that of all his holdings, he wanted only one: a failing city newspaper called the Clarion. He moved in, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Then he hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line, as if journalism were a conquest and he had taken the city's flag.

He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece, and for a time the marriage gleamed. But a run of breakfast-table scenes charted its cooling — two people reading separate newspapers in silence, the space between them widening until it held no sound at all.

Then one day on the street, mud on his coat from a passing carriage, Emmett met a shopgirl named Nora Kell, and something shifted. He began visiting her rooms in secret, and the secret became the only warm thing in his life.

Mid-campaign for governor, the party boss Halloran brought Adele to Nora's rooms and threatened exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw. He lost the election. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and the marriage collapsed.

Emmett married Nora. Almost immediately, he forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice. Her debut was a humiliation, and Devlin — drunk, savage, back in the city for the night — began a review so cruel that Emmett finished it himself, printed it, and fired Devlin for writing what he himself had completed.

Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again, and Emmett finally let her stop.

He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall, fitting pieces together that never seemed to form a whole. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel she could not take back, Nora packed and left him.

Emmett wrecked her bedroom that night. He found a glass snow globe on the dresser, turned it in his hands, and murmured *Bluebell*. He carried it past the endless mirrors, into the silence that became his life.

Nash read Barrow's memoir. He interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora again, and the butler Colm. Each gave him a different Emmett — the tyrant, the idealist, the lover, the corpse. He wrote his piece concluding that no single word explains a life, and filed it. In the basement of Silvermount, workmen shoveled a child's wooden sled — the name *Bluebell* burned into its runners — into the furnace, and the fire took it without comment.

In a flat two stories above the street, an old man sat across from a younger one, turning a glass of whiskey slowly in his fingers. The curtains were open. Below, blue and red lights smeared across the pavement. The old man gestured vaguely toward the window. "You see that? All of it. The concrete, the glass, the flesh. Nothing survives time. Not the buildings. Not the people inside them. Not what they did or what they failed to do." The younger man said nothing. The old man sipped. "We like to think otherwise. But time eats everything. It eats the crime and it eats the punishment and it eats the memory of both."

Down on the street, police led two men out of a club in handcuffs. One of them, Cort, had his arm hanging wrong, bent at a place where there was no joint. His face was swollen and slack. The other, Jonah, had blood spattered up his forearms and across his shirt in a fine spray, as though he had been caught in a sudden rust-colored rain. They did not look at each other. They did not speak. Officers pushed their heads down as they were folded into separate cars, and the doors shut with the heavy finality of safes closing.

The man beneath him had already stopped resisting, but Jonah kept going, his jaw clenched, his eyes flat and distant. Cort lay on the floor nearby, cradling his snapped arm, watching. And a few feet away, leaning against the bar with a drink in his hand, the real Adder observed the whole scene with the mild interest of a man watching television.

This had begun with Cort moving through the club's rooms, shoving past bodies, peering into faces. He seized a man by the collar who he was certain was the Adder. The man was not. The man twisted Cort's arm behind him and snapped it with a short, professional motion, like breaking a breadstick. Cort dropped to his knees, and Jonah came running.

Before the club, before any of that, two men had stopped Cort and Jonah on the street outside the party. They offered a name. They offered directions. A place called the Pit. "He'll be there," one of them said. "He's always there." They smiled the way people smile when they are selling something that costs more than money.

Before that, Cort and Jonah had stumbled out of the party and found Lise being lifted onto a stretcher. Her face was unrecognizable. Paramedics moved with controlled urgency, and the ambulance doors opened like a mouth preparing to swallow her whole. Cort had stood frozen. Jonah had put his hand over his own mouth.

Earlier still, in a pedestrian underpass, Lise had been trying to avoid a busy road. She had left the party alone, disgusted by Cort's behavior, and had chosen the tunnel rather than wait for traffic. Inside, she found a man called the Adder beating a transsexual woman. He stopped. He turned. He saw Lise. He raped her there on the concrete, and when she tried to scream, he slammed her skull against the ground. A passer-by appeared at the mouth of the tunnel, saw what was happening, and backed away into the night as though he had accidentally opened the wrong door.

Before the underpass, before the party, there had been the underground train. Lise, Cort, and Jonah riding together, shouting over the noise about sex and about Cort's drinking. Jonah teasing. Cort defensive. Lise between them, laughing despite herself, one hand resting on her stomach where something was growing that she had not yet told them about.

And before that night, before the train, there had been mornings. Lise lying in bed with Cort, telling him about a dream. A red tunnel. She described it and he made a joke about Jonah, her ex, and she laughed and hit his chest, and the dream dissolved into daylight and warmth and the ordinary sounds of the flat.

And before the dream, there had been a morning alone in that flat. Lise holding a plastic stick in the bathroom, watching two lines appear. Positive. She sat on the edge of the tub for a long time.

And before that, a park. Sprinklers turning. Children running through them. Lise on a bench with a book she was not reading, one hand resting on her stomach, feeling the first faint sense that everything was already beginning to end.

# The Junction

The red light meant nothing. Ruben had the pedal down and Pipo beside him and blood still on his hands, and when the small car entered the junction he never even touched the brake. The impact spun both vehicles into a shrieking halt, glass and coolant pooling on the asphalt. He'd been running before the crash, and the crash was just another kind of running.

He had started running because of the house. The cramped rooms he shared with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma, and their baby. Thin walls. Thin patience. Nestor robbed a pharmacy by night and came home smelling of adrenaline and chemical dust, and when Alma said something wrong he beat her until the baby woke screaming. Afterward, in the kitchen's blue dark, Ruben would press her. Come with me. Take the baby. We'll go south. She only shook her head, but her eyes stayed on him a beat too long.

He found Tigre in the yard one morning, the rottweiler standing over a neighbor's dog with its throat open. Nestor's dog, but Nestor never walked it. Ruben started entering Tigre in the local dogfights, and the wins came steady and easy, money stacking in a tin behind the water heater. Tigre killed without hesitation. Ruben recognized something in that.

When he paid two thugs to beat Nestor in an alley, Nestor came home with a split lip and a new understanding of things. He took Alma, the baby, and Ruben's tin of savings and vanished. The house went quiet. Ruben kept fighting Tigre because it was all he had left. The last fight was the biggest purse. The promoter Chaco worked the crowd, took his cut, and when Tigre started losing, Chaco shot the dog in the ring. Ruben crossed the distance with a blade and opened Chaco's throat. Pipo pulled him out through the back. They ran for the car.

Nestor surfaced months later, shot dead robbing a bank. At the funeral Alma stood by the grave with the baby on her hip. Ruben made his last offer. She looked through him. "I'm not going anywhere with you," she said. "Not now. Not ever."

---

The billboard had been Hector's idea. He'd walked out on his wife and two daughters for Celine Vaz, whose body sold perfume across the city's skyline, and he moved her into a new flat where she could see herself from the window—ten meters tall, flawless, untouchable. She'd liked it at first. Then she understood it was a cage made of glass and admiration.

She woke in hospital with her leg pinned together in steel rods, the crash a blank space in her memory. Pinned but healing, they said. Her lapdog Chispa was lost somewhere in the new flat, and Hector promised to find her. He tore up the floorboards calling her name while Celine's leg, beneath its cast, began to darken and stink. Gangrene, the doctors said. Chispa had fallen through a hole in the floor and wandered the building's crawlspace, whimpering just out of reach. They amputated the leg above the knee. A week later, the billboard came down. Her face vanished from the skyline. Hector stayed, but something in his eyes had changed—he was already looking toward a door.

---

The businessman Elian found Cardo sleeping under a bridge and offered him money to murder his half-brother Sergio, his business partner, his rival. Cardo took the contract. He took all contracts. A former guerrilla who'd never found his way back to the world, he lived among strays—dogs and men alike—taking work that required no name.

That same week he stood at the edge of a cemetery and watched his estranged wife lowered into the earth. He'd been gone twenty-three years. Afterward he followed his grown daughter Perla home, watching from across the street as she entered a flat building in a part of the city he'd never known.

It was at the junction where Ruben's car came to rest that Cardo found Tigre. The bleeding rottweiler was half-dead in the wreckage, and Cardo dragged him out by his hindquarters, carried him to his lair, and nursed him back to health among his own pack of strays. Tigre healed fast. One afternoon while Cardo was out, Tigre killed every other dog in the yard. Cardo came home to silence and blood and pressed his gun to the dog's skull. The dog looked at him. Cardo couldn't fire.

He abducted Sergio that week but chained him in the lair instead of killing him. Then he called Elian and brought the brothers face to face. He set a loaded pistol between them on a crate, took money from both, and walked out.

That night he broke into Perla's flat. He stood in her kitchen, touching a mug, a dish towel. He spoke into her answering machine—a long, halting confession of who he was, what he'd done, why he'd left. He took her photograph from the wall.

By morning he was shaved and wearing clean clothes. He left his money in an envelope on her doorstep. Then he walked out into the wasteland beyond the city's edge, Tigre at his side, and did not look back.

Tobias skipped work on an impulse he couldn't name. The train rocked him past suburbs and scrubland to the end of the rail line, a seaside town he had no memory of visiting. On the frozen sand, a woman stood watching the gray water. She turned and smiled as though she'd been waiting. "Ivy," she said, offering her name like a gift.

They drove back to the city together in her car, and at a traffic light she reached over and squeezed his hand. "Come up," she said when they reached her building. He followed without hesitation.

He'd first seen that face weeks earlier, in a bookshop. She'd been behind the counter, ringing up a young man's purchase, laughing at something he said. When Tobias approached, she gave him the same polite blankness she gave any stranger. The young man's name was Peck, and Ivy touched his wrist while making change.

That blankness had been purchased. Ivy had walked into a memory-erasure clinic and paid to have every trace of Tobias dissolved from her mind.

Nina and Grady showed him the form letter. Tobias read it twice, then drove to the clinic and demanded the same procedure from its director, Dr. Hallam, who studied him with clinical calm and said, "Bring us everything."

So Tobias boxed up every object connected with Ivy. The scarf she'd left behind, a coffee mug, a movie stub. He sealed the cardboard and handed it over so the clinic could map the memories attached to them.

That night, technicians Dell and Peck—the same Peck from the bookshop—rigged the equipment in Tobias's flat. Peck handled the mementos with conspicuous care, slipping two into his jacket pocket when Dell turned away.

Inside his own head, Tobias watched the most recent and ugliest memories dissolve. Ivy coming home drunk, the dent in his car's fender like a wound. The fight that escalated from the driveway to the kitchen, her voice splitting into fury, her walking out the door for good.

Before that fight: the months of curdling. Recrimination over her drinking, over his withholding, the silences that lasted days. Each dissolved in pale light, pixel by pixel.

On his bed, Dell and the receptionist Rosa shared a joint and lost track of the monitors. Tobias's memory map went off the rails, scenes bleeding into one another.

He reached the memories he loved and fought to keep them. The ice on the frozen river when they'd skated until their ankles ached. The noodle house, steam fogging the windows. The drive-in, her head on his shoulder. He tried to smuggle her into memories she was never part of—hiding her in a childhood bedroom, tucking her into a school field trip—desperate to preserve her somewhere the erasure couldn't reach.

Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure, and Rosa kissed him in the hallway. Hallam's wife appeared behind them, holding a clinic form letter. "She doesn't remember your affair," his wife said. "You erased it from her too."

The erasure pulled Tobias further back. A beach party at the end of the rail line. A seaside town. He and Ivy breaking into an empty house on the shore, laughing, lying on the floor under a stranger's roof.

In the last surviving memory, that same empty house, they stood together. She told him goodbye. She told him to meet her at the beach.

The erasure completed. Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy had ever existed, and went to work, and felt nothing, and on an impulse he couldn't name, skipped it.

Weeks later, Rosa quit the clinic and mailed files and session tapes back to every patient on the books.

In Ivy's flat, the package arrived. They put the tape in her player and listened to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart. She ran. She came back. They stood in the doorway, the tape still playing, and agreed to try anyway.

The derelict building smelled of rust and old smoke. Roy Mercer stood in the doorway, hands raised, mouth forming the word *listen*—but Martin Kray had listened enough. The Polaroid was already in his left hand. The gun in his right. The flash of the shot was the last thing he would remember; the photograph developing between his fingers was the proof he would carry forward, a fresh fact in a world that dissolved every few minutes. Roy's body settled against the concrete wall. Martin shook the photo and waited for the image to fix.

---

A motel room he did not remember checking into. A phone pressed to his ear. An anonymous voice on the other end, patient, asking questions. Martin told the story of Elias Prine—the claimant he had interviewed a lifetime ago, the man whose memory loss he had ruled psychosomatic, whose claim he had denied. He told it because the voice asked, and because telling was the only way he knew, now, to hold a thought.

---

Corinne slid a printed vehicle registry record across the bar. The name on it was Roy Mercer. Martin stared at the letters. They meant nothing to him, but the licence plate number matched the one inked on his thigh, and the system did not lie. Facts were facts. He folded the paper and pocketed it.

---

Elias Prine had sat across the desk in a pressed grey suit, calm and articulate, describing gaps in his memory with the composure of a man reciting weather. Martin had seen dozens like him. He wrote *psychosomatic* in the adjudication box and denied the claim. Open and shut.

---

Vance went down hard against the motel bathroom tile. Martin stood over him, breathing through his mouth, the gun steady. He did not know what Vance had done. He knew only that a bruised woman had given him this name, and that was enough. He marched Vance outside and forced him into the passenger seat, driving him out of town under a sky turning the colour of old paper.

---

Elias's wife was diabetic. She tested him, asking for injection after injection, and he complied each time as though it were the first. By the time the paramedics arrived she was cold. He could not tell them how many doses he had given her. He could not tell them anything at all.

---

Corinne hid every pen in the house. She stood close, speaking slowly, repeating accusations until the words became meaningless and the frustration crested. When he struck her she did not flinch. She studied the mark on her cheekbone in the hallway mirror, then left. She returned an hour later with a swollen lip and a name. *Vance*, she said. A man who deserved to be found.

---

The system was simple. Instant photographs, annotated notes, tattoos for the facts that mattered. Martin had built it in the weeks after the bathroom attack, after the second intruder escaped and the doctors told him his brain would no longer hold new experience. Each tattoo was a fixed point. Each photograph was a door into a room he would never otherwise know he had entered.

---

Corinne recognised the suit the moment he walked in. The dead man's clothes hung slightly wrong on Martin's frame, and the sports car in the lot confirmed what she already suspected. She served him a beer without comment. In the kitchen, the staff took turns spitting into the glass before she carried it out.

---

The bathroom was steam and broken glass. Two men had come through the door. Martin had killed the first with a razor shard from the sink. The second swung a torch into his skull, and the world narrowed to a white point, then nothing. When he woke, his wife was on the tiles. The second man was gone. The nothing kept expanding.

---

The tattoo artist worked in silence. Martin watched the needle trace the licence plate characters into his thigh, the sixth fact, the next fixed point. The pain was irrelevant. Pain he could remember. It was everything after that dissolved.

---

He burned her hairbrush and her books in a field at dusk. The smoke rose straight in the still air. He sat beside the fire until it died, trying to feel the shape of what he had lost, knowing that by morning the grief would be gone and he would have to find it again from scratch.

---

The voice on the phone gave him a name and a location. Gil Marsh. Drug dealer. The man he was looking for. Martin wrote it on a photograph of the motel room and placed it in his breast pocket.

---

The basement was derelict and cold. Gil Marsh fought, but Martin was larger and angrier and driven by facts he could not question. He beat the man until he stopped moving, then strangled him with his own belt. He photographed the body and stood in the silence that followed.

---

Gil was dying. His lips moved. *Elias*, he whispered. The name meant nothing to Martin. He changed into the dead man's suit, took his keys, and drove the sports car into the night.

---

Roy arrived at the derelict building the next day, or the next hour—Martin could not be sure. Roy spoke calmly. Gil was innocent. Martin had already avenged his wife, a year ago, with Roy's help. And Martin himself was the man in the Prine story. Elias. The name Gil had whispered.

---

A year before the main action, Roy had found the real attacker. A plainclothes officer with a patient voice, Roy had guided Martin to the man, and Martin had killed him. Within minutes the memory was gone. The killing existed only in a photograph Martin no longer trusted.

---

Martin looked at Roy's face. He looked at the photographs spread on the floor. He picked up the image of Gil's body and held a flame to it, watching it curl. On Roy's photograph he wrote *he is lying to you*. Then he copied down the licence plate number from Roy's car and placed it in his pocket, beside the other facts, the only things he could believe.

Corinne hid every pen in the house. She stood close, speaking slowly, repeating accusations until the words became meaningless and the frustration crested. When he struck her she did not flinch. She studied the mark on her cheekbone in the hallway mirror, then left. She returned an hour later with a swollen lip and a name. *Vance*, she said. A man who deserved to be found.

---

The system was simple. Instant photographs, annotated notes, tattoos for the facts that mattered. Martin had built it in the weeks after the bathroom attack, after the second intruder escaped and the doctors told him his brain would no longer hold new experience. Each tattoo was a fixed point. Each photograph was a door into a room he would never otherwise know he had entered.

---

Corinne recognised the suit the moment he walked in. The dead man's clothes hung slightly wrong on Martin's frame, and the sports car in the lot confirmed what she already suspected. She served him a beer without comment. In the kitchen, the staff took turns spitting into the glass before she carried it out.

---

The bathroom was steam and broken glass. Two men had come through the door. Martin had killed the first with a razor shard from the sink. The second swung a torch into his skull, and the world narrowed to a white point, then nothing. When he woke, his wife was on the tiles. The second man was gone. The nothing kept expanding.

---

The tattoo artist worked in silence. Martin watched the needle trace the licence plate characters into his thigh, the sixth fact, the next fixed point. The pain was irrelevant. Pain he could remember. It was everything after that dissolved.

---

He burned her hairbrush and her books in a field at dusk. The smoke rose straight in the still air. He sat beside the fire until it died, trying to feel the shape of what he had lost, knowing that by morning the grief would be gone and he would have to find it again from scratch.

---

The voice on the phone gave him a name and a location. Gil Marsh. Drug dealer. The man he was looking for. Martin wrote it on a photograph of the motel room and placed it in his breast pocket.

---

The basement was derelict and cold. Gil Marsh fought, but Martin was larger and angrier and driven by facts he could not question. He beat the man until he stopped moving, then strangled him with his own belt. He photographed the body and stood in the silence that followed.

---

Gil was dying. His lips moved. *Elias*, he whispered. The name meant nothing to Martin. He changed into the dead man's suit, took his keys, and drove the sports car into the night.

---

Roy arrived at the derelict building the next day, or the next hour—Martin could not be sure. Roy spoke calmly. Gil was innocent. Martin had already avenged his wife, a year ago, with Roy's help. And Martin himself was the man in the Prine story. Elias. The name Gil had whispered.

---

A year before the main action, Roy had found the real attacker. A plainclothes officer with a patient voice, Roy had guided Martin to the man, and Martin had killed him. Within minutes the memory was gone. The killing existed only in a photograph Martin no longer trusted.

---

Martin looked at Roy's face. He looked at the photographs spread on the floor. He picked up the image of Gil's body and held a flame to it, watching it curl. On Roy's photograph he wrote *he is lying to you*. Then he copied down the licence plate number from Roy's car and placed it in his pocket, beside the other facts, the only things he could believe.

The gun was cold against his teeth and the taste of metal was the taste of every sleepless night he had ever suffered. He pulled the trigger. The bullet tore through his cheek and out the back of Rex Marrow's skull, and Rex—his other self, his sleepwalking shadow—crumpled down the stairwell without a sound. The pain was enormous and clarifying. Blood pooled in his mouth. He spat it onto the concrete and waited for the person he had been to stay dead.

It had started with insomnia. Years of it. A product-recall investigator who could not sleep, who tried every pill and every clinic, and found that the only thing that worked was crying. Support groups for diseases he did not have. Testicular cancer, blood parasites, brain parasites. He would sit in a circle of the dying and weep for an hour and then sleep like a stone. It was repulsive and it saved him.

Then Ada Vey started showing up. She wore too much makeup and laughed at the wrong moments and her suffering was obviously, painfully performed. Her presence infected the room. The other members noticed. The release curdled. He stopped sleeping again.

On a red-eye flight for a recall case he sat next to a man named Rex Marrow who sold soap. Rex talked the whole flight about fat and lye and the lies printed on packaging. He pressed a business card into the narrator's hand. The narrator pocketed it and forgot about it.

Then his flat exploded. Everything he owned—every catalogue bookshelf, every catalogue plate—gone in a flash of gas and broken glass. He stood outside the wreckage in his work clothes and dialled the only number he still had. Rex answered. Within the hour Rex had him inside a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, paper peeling from the walls, water staining the ceilings.

Outside a bar that first night Rex asked him to hit him as hard as he could. He did. They beat each other bloody in the car park, and for the first time in months he felt something genuine move through his body.

Two men brawling became a weekly basement club with rules. No shirts, no shoes. They fought until one man went limp or called stop. Word spread. Members came. The basement filled with blood and breathing.

Then Ada overdosed. Rex found her and brought her back to the house. Within days the two of them were loud and constant, and the narrator could not stand the sound of it through the thin walls.

Rex rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He called it the finest product in the world. The narrator watched him stir the vat and felt the heat on his face.

Rex pressed lye to the back of the narrator's hand and held him there. The pain was a white blade. The narrator tried to retreat into his old meditation, his cave, his power animal. Rex would not let him. The scar stayed.

The narrator used his beaten face as evidence and blackmailed his employer into paying him to stay away. The cheques came every week. He did not go to the office again.

Rex turned the club into an organisation he called Havoc. Shaven-headed recruits filled the house. They took orders. They vandalised corporate property. The narrator watched the thing he had built become something else.

Then Rex steered the car into oncoming traffic, let it roll, and vanished.

A member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation. The narrator tried to shut it down. He travelled city to city and found identical clubs everywhere, men who greeted him as Rex Marrow.

He understood. He and Rex were the same person. Rex had been acting while he slept.

Ada confirmed it. She had been sleeping with him.

He discovered Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. He climbed the stairwell to defuse the charges. Rex met him there. The gun. The stairwell. The shot.

The shaven recruits delivered Ada to the tower. She found him bleeding and alive. They held hands at the window as the buildings came down.

In a bar two years after everything had quietly ended, Odile sat across from Wilder and told him her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night, she said, confessing everything to Emlyn. Wilder held his glass and studied her face for some sign of what this confession had cost her, but she gave him only the calm, flat delivery of someone reading items from a list. She said Emlyn had listened. She said he had not raised his voice. She did not say whether he had forgiven her, and Wilder did not ask.

Then, almost as an afterthought, Odile let slip that Emlyn had been publishing a writer whom Wilder represented—a novelist the two men had always quietly detested, a man whose sentences they had once taken apart over drinks with a shared, almost conjugal contempt. Wilder felt something tighten in his chest. He saw the arrangement suddenly for what it was: not a coincidence but a message, Emlyn's slow and patient reply to a confession that had apparently been delivered only the night before, though the silence around it had clearly been years in the making.

Wilder rang Emlyn in a state. His voice broke on the first attempt and he had to begin again. Emlyn answered on the third ring and listened without interrupting, then said he would come to the house the same evening.

He came. He stood in the hallway with his coat still buttoned and said he had known for four years. His wife had told him on the trip abroad. He said it the way one might report a change in the weather—without emphasis, without grievance. And then, as though clearing away the last of it, he added that he had never thought much of his friend's letters either. Wilder understood then that Emlyn had read them, or at least had held one in his hand long enough to judge the handwriting, and that the judgement had been passed long ago and stored without decay.

All of this had come after the rooms. The rented rooms in the quiet district, which Wilder and Odile had once filled with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own—those rooms had become a chore before the end. They split the crockery between them with a care that felt more final than any argument. She took the blue-rimmed plates. He took the cups. They surrendered the lease and did not embrace in the street outside.

Before that, there had been dinners at the married couple's house. The two men would discuss racquet games and schoolboy sport, trading memories of fives and cross-country runs with a fluency that excluded Odile entirely. She would sit at her own table with no part in the talk, watching the performance of a friendship that had survived what she and Wilder had built beside it.

Before that, the hotel abroad. Emlyn had asked about a letter held for her at the desk, addressed in a hand he recognised. He said it calmly, over breakfast, as though mentioning the weather or the price of the room. Odile looked at the letter and then at her husband and understood that the question was not really a question.

She confessed. She told him about the rooms, the quiet district, the crockery. Emlyn listened and then remarked, with a gentleness that was worse than anger, that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Odile went back to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever about the trip. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had. Wilder made tea. She sat in the chair by the window. Neither of them touched, and neither of them spoke of what was already beginning to end.

Before that, Emlyn had drunk through a long restaurant lunch with Wilder, baiting him about contemporary fiction, naming authors and titles with a precision that Wilder found unsettling, and never once mentioning what he had learned. Wilder came away from the table with the sense of having been examined, though he could not have said by what.

And before all of it—before the rooms, the trip, the confession, the years of quiet knowledge—there had been a party at the house of Wilder's closest friend. Wilder had led Odile upstairs to a quiet room while the other guests drank below, and he had told her how lovely she was. She had looked at him for a long moment, and then she had not looked away.

He was conscripted as a chaplain's assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. They gave him a helmet and a Bible and put him on a ship and that was more or less the whole of his preparation. He had been taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet with a film actress. This had happened, or would happen, or was always happening. The aliens had no use for clocks. The actress had no use for him. They lay together on a geodesic dome under a canopy of three moons and he tried to explain that he had not asked to be there, and she said nobody ever asked to be anywhere.

A boy was born in a small industrial town and grew into a weak, peculiar child. His mother said he had the look of a child who had seen something he shouldn't have. His father said nothing. The father had opinions about how boys should be raised and they were not gentle opinions.

He was sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. The hooks were still in the ceilings. The drains still smelled of blood. The guards did not speak his language and he did not speak theirs and this was fine. Communication would not have improved anything.

He came home, collapsed, and was hospitalised, where another patient introduced him to a hack science fiction writer. The writer had a theory about time. The writer had a theory about everything. The writer's books had covers with rocket ships on them and women with brassieres shaped like hubcaps. The writer told him that time was not a river but a mountain range, and that every moment existed simultaneously, and that the dead were not dead, only elsewhere. He listened. He had nowhere else to be.

The aliens explained that every moment exists at once and that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet. They said this the way someone might explain that water is wet. They were patient. They had had this conversation with many creatures from many worlds and the creatures from his world were always the most upset by it.

He was lost behind the lines with a scout who beat him for wanting to be left to die. The scout was a large man with strong opinions about survival. He had no opinions about anything. The scout dragged him through the woods by his collar and cursed him in a language he almost understood.

He married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school and became rich. The daughter was kind and plain and had a slight squint that the marriage would eventually correct, or not correct, or had already corrected. They had children. The children grew up. The money accumulated. The prescriptions paid for everything.

The city was destroyed by fire in one night, and the prisoners in the meat locker came up to find it gone. There was nothing where the city had been. The sky was the colour of a bruise. The air was thick with ash and the ash was thick with people, or what had been people. He stood in the street and did not know what street it was because there were no streets anymore.

His daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands. She had a lawyer. She had opinions. She said it was for his own good. She said this while looking at him with the corrected squint that made her eyes seem perpetually aimed at something just past his left ear.

His father threw him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim, and he sank to the bottom. He sat on the tile and watched the light move on the surface above him. It was peaceful. A man reached in and pulled him out. His father was disappointed.

The pair were captured, and the scout died of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last breath. The scout's hand was black up to the elbow. The scout said it was his fault for being weak. The scout said this with a kind of conviction that made it sound like a compliment. Then the scout was elsewhere.

He went on a radio talk show and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. The host was patient. The callers were less patient. One caller said he should be committed. Another caller said he should be shot. He agreed with both callers, in principle, though not in sequence.

The prisoners were made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves. The digger was a man he had known, or would know, or had always known. They carried the digger out with the bodies and there was no distinction made between them.

He survived an air crash in the mountains, and his wife died of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital. She had been rushing. The snow was deep. The car's tailpipe was blocked. She died in the driver's seat with her foot on the brake and her eyes open, looking at something he would never see.

He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. The officers were fat and complacent. They played cards. They complained about the food. He ate what they discarded and was grateful.

He was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he had always known he would be. The beam made a sound like a door closing. The crowd made a sound like a door opening. He had said what he came to say. He had always known he would say it.

A fellow prisoner promised to have him killed one day on the dead scout's account. The prisoner was a small man with a thin face and a long memory. He said it quietly, the way someone might state the time of day. He said it as though it were already true, and perhaps it was.

Detective Isaiah Reece had worked enough highway shoulders to know the posture of the dead. What he was not prepared for, kneeling in the gravel with his badge still swinging from his neck, was the face. He turned the body gently and the world narrowed to a point. Kwame. His brother Kwame, grown into a man Reece had never bothered to find, laid out among the litter and crushed grass like something discarded. He did not scream. He placed his hand on his brother's chest and said nothing at all, because there was no one yet to hear him.

Weeks earlier, in a part of the city where the light seemed always to be failing, an immigrant shopkeeper named Nadir stood beside his daughter Sahar in a gun dealer's cramped back room. The dealer watched Nadir's lips shape the English words and smirked at each one that came out wrong. Sahar said nothing. She held her father's arm and studied the revolver as though it were a piece of fruit she was deciding whether to buy.

That same week, Trey and Kwame slid into the prosecutor Halstead's idling sedan while Halstead was still inside the restaurant signing his check. They were gone before the valet noticed the empty space.

At the Halstead house, Paula stood in the doorway with her arms crossed while the locksmith Mateo knelt at the deadbolt. She spoke loudly, as though volume might make her suspicions true, telling anyone within earshot that this man was certainly a gang affiliate who would duplicate her keys and sell them on the street. Mateo kept working. He had heard worse.

Officer Boyle pulled the Hobarts over on a pretext that was not a pretext at all but a hunger. He made Clay stand at the rear bumper while he patted down Renee with hands that lingered in places a pat-down could never justify. Clay watched. Renee did not speak. Boyle let them go with a warning, and the silence in the car afterward was the loudest sound either of them had ever endured.

Boyle's partner Voss requested a new patrol car the next morning. Not a transfer, he told the commander—just a different car, a different partner, anything that did not require sitting next to that man another shift. The commander said he would see what he could do.

Mateo replaced the lock on Nadir's shop next and pointed to the door frame, which had warped away from the jamb. He told Nadir the door itself needed replacing. Nadir studied the gap and told Mateo he was running a con, that the door was fine, that he would not pay for work that was not broken.

Boyle sat across from a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank and begged her to authorize his father's treatment. She reviewed the file, closed it, and told him the claim was denied. He asked her what he was supposed to do. She did not answer, because there was no answer that would satisfy him.

Nadir's shop was smashed that night. The door gave way with one kick. Glass, shelves, register—everything taken or broken. When he filed the claim, the insurer pointed to the locksmith's notation about the door and refused to pay.

Trey and Kwame, still driving stolen cars like they were borrowed, struck a shopkeeper named Pham in a crosswalk. They panicked, loaded him into the back seat, and dumped him outside the nearest hospital before speeding away.

On a stretch of highway no one could later identify precisely, Renee Hobart hung upside down in her seatbelt while fire climbed the windshield. The officer who crawled through the broken glass and pulled her free was Boyle. She saw his face before she lost consciousness and understood that the world was not a place where justice lived.

Clay Hobart was stopped mid-carjacking of his own recovered vehicle, and Voss arrived in time to talk the responding officers down from their triggers. Later, Clay drove Trey at speed away from a police pursuit and, at the last moment, braked and shoved him out onto the pavement.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house in the dark. When Mateo appeared in the doorway, Nadir raised the revolver and fired just as a small girl—Rosie—ran into her father's arms. The shot echoed. The helicopters came with the dark, sweeping over every neighbourhood in long, methodical passes, spraying the city for crop pests. The chemical mist settled on rooftops and car bonnets, on sleeping children and wakeful insomniacs, on dogs chained in yards and on lovers tangled in sheets. By dawn the smell had seeped into everything, a sweet chemical ghost that lingered for days.

Doctor Neil Hartigan stood before the bathroom mirror knotting his tie while his wife Bess, a painter, held two dresses up to herself in the doorway. She chose the blue one. They had a dinner party to attend and she wanted to look right for it, though she would later admit that looking right had never been her strong suit.

Across town, in a flat that smelled of stale coffee and plug-in air freshener, Cheryl pressed the phone to her ear and talked a man in Toowoomba through his fantasy involving a swimming pool and a woman in rubber gloves. Her husband Stu sat on the sofa beside her, seething, watching a cricket match with the sound off. He could hear every word she said. He always could.

At the Blue Note, the singer Vida closed her eyes around a slow ballad while her cellist daughter Bee sat alone in their kitchen, sawing through a Bach suite for an audience of nobody. Bee played until her fingers ached, then sat in the silence that followed, which was worse.

Officer Rowe parked his patrol car on a dead-end street and opened the back door. The family dog, a elderly kelpie named Rex, looked up at him with trusting brown eyes. Rowe had told Peg the dog had run off. It was easier than explaining where he'd actually been that afternoon, easier than explaining Nan. He closed the door and drove away. The dog watched him go, then lay down on the kerb and waited for someone who would not come back.

A waitress called Rhona was running late for her shift, reaching for her handbag on the passenger seat, when the boy stepped off the kerb. Charlie Rill rolled across the bonnet and hit the road hard. He stood up, brushed himself off, and told her he was fine. He walked home insisting on it, told his mother he was fine, sat at the breakfast table and said it again. Then his eyes rolled back and he was gone.

That same morning, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake. Charlie Rill, the boy's mother said on the phone. He'll be eight on Saturday. Otto wrote it down carefully on his order pad, the name and the age and the request for chocolate icing, and then he waited for the day that would never come.

Charlie collapsed into a coma and his parents Grant and Elaine kept vigil at the hospital, sleeping in chairs and waking to the beep of monitors. They barely spoke. They held hands across the narrow bed and waited.

At the Hartigan house, Ike and Dot house-sat and passed the time by photographing Dot made up as a beaten corpse. They arranged her on the kitchen floor, on the stairs, in the bathtub. They developed the photos in Neil's makeshift darkroom and laughed at how real she looked.

Stu and three friends drove out to fish the Kandos River and found a young woman's body floating face down in the shallows. They stood on the bank and stared at her for a long time. Then Stu tied a rope around her ankle and tethered her to a fallen log. They carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone.

When Nan's ex-husband Cass heard she had a new man, he drove to her place with a handsaw and took everything apart. The sofa, the bed frame, the dining chairs. He left the pieces in a neat pile on the front lawn and flew back to base.

Unpaid and ignored, Otto Kemp began making anonymous phone calls to the Rill household. He breathed into the receiver. He said things he would later wish he hadn't. Nobody answered. Nobody ever answered.

Vern's wife Iris, a party clown, sat in her costume with the makeup still on and listened to Vern describe what the men had done at the river. She stared at him. She said nothing for a very long time. Then she said, "You left her there. You fished."

At the dinner party, Bess had too much wine and admitted to a nude modelling session from years ago and an affair that had gone with it. Neil set down his glass carefully and made a scene that ended the evening. They drove home in silence.

Charlie died in hospital. Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to confront Otto, who they somehow knew had been calling. But when they got there, Otto pulled a loaf of warm bread from the oven, cut it, and fed them slice after slice. He grieved with them. They sat together and wept and ate and none of them could say why.

Bee found her mother asleep on the sofa. She closed the garage door, started the car, and lay down on the concrete beside it. The engine ran and ran.

At a picnic in the hills, Stu picked up a rock and brought it down on a young woman's head. He did it the way he did everything, without hesitation and without remorse.

A tremor shook the entire city. Buildings cracked. Car alarms screamed. And every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin, read by a woman with steady hands and a calm voice, as though the world had not shifted beneath them all.

Solly Two Coats dressed his crew in the long black coats and wide-brimmed hats of devout pilgrims. In the grey light of a northern port, they walked into the diamond house with prayer books in their hands and walked out with a stone the size of a pigeon's egg nestled in a silk-lined case. Nobody questioned holy men.

Meanwhile, in another part of the country, the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby had their own problems. They sent Pretty Sam, their best man, down to a camp of travellers to buy a caravan. Sam was a bruiser, thick through the neck, and he figured he could intimidate the travellers into a cheap price. But he hadn't counted on Finn, a bare-knuckle fighter who'd been born in that camp and didn't take kindly to threats. Finn put Sam down with one punch that cracked the silence like a whip, and left him senseless in the mud. Halloway was now without a fighter for the fixed bout he'd promised the gang boss Coldstone.

Word reached Solly overseas. His cousin Marv, who ran things from warmer climates, told him to bring the stone straight over. No detours, no middlemen. Straight over.

Halloway had no choice but to approach Finn. He offered the traveller money and promises, and put him in the fight against Coldstone's man. He looked Coldstone in the eye and swore Finn would go down in the fourth round. Coldstone nodded once, and that was the deal.

Back in the port, Grigor the Nail was weaving his own web. He told Solly about a bookmaker's in the city where the odds were good and the doors were unwatched. Simultaneously, he tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno—told them exactly where Solly would be and when.

Solly landed in the city and went straight to the fence Hersch. He handed over the stone, collected what he was owed, and headed for the bookmaker's to put it all on the fight.

But Finn didn't go down in the fourth. He knocked his opponent out cold in the first round, and the arena went silent. Coldstone lost a fortune. He found Halloway afterward and broke two of his fingers for every round Finn had promised to last.

At the bookmaker's, Ike, Benno and a man called Tulley made their move. They bungled it from the start—knocked over a table, drew a gun too soon—but they grabbed Solly by the arm and took his case before Grigor chased them off into the alleys. They had the case. They didn't have the stone.

Marv flew in that night and found Solly's room empty and his cousin gone. He hired a bounty hunter called Ledge, a man with a flat stare and steady hands, and told him to find Solly and find the stone.

Grigor found Solly first. He took him to a basement and cut off his arm at the elbow to make a point about loyalty, then pried open the case. It was empty. The stone was not inside.

Coldstone got hold of Solly after that. He fed him to his pigs
